description: Applies principles from "A Philosophy of Software Design" to architecture, module and API boundaries, and consequential refactors. Use for architecture planning, module or API design, design review, or diagnosing shallow modules, information leakage, and pass-through layers.
---

# Software Design

Apply these principles when architecture or abstraction quality is a material part of the task.

## Two Modes

### Writing New Code

Apply these principles in order of impact.

#### Think strategically

Invest in design instead of stopping when the code first works. Produce a clean design that works, and spend 10–20% of the effort on design improvements.

#### Create deep modules

Each module should provide powerful functionality behind a simple interface. A few deep methods beat many shallow ones. Ask whether the interface is simpler than the implementation.

#### Hide information

Each module should encapsulate design decisions that remain invisible through its interface. If one decision appears in several modules, reorganize the code until that decision has one home.

#### Make interfaces general-purpose

Design an interface broad enough to support current uses while keeping its functionality focused. Ask for the simplest interface that covers every current need.

#### Give each layer a different abstraction

Adjacent layers should operate at different abstraction levels. Remove pass-through methods that delegate with the same signature.

#### Pull complexity downwards

Handle complexity inside the module instead of pushing it to callers. A simple interface matters more than a simple implementation.

#### Define errors out of existence

Redefine APIs so avoidable error conditions cannot arise. Mask low-level exceptions and consolidate their handling. Reserve crashes for unrecoverable failures.

#### Design it twice

Consider at least two radically different approaches before committing. Compare their strengths and costs. Apply this comparison to interfaces and implementations, then consider the broader system decomposition.

#### Name precisely

Names should create a clear mental image of an entity's purpose. Avoid vague choices such as `data`, `result`, `info`, or `tmp`. Name booleans with predicates such as `isConnected` instead of a state label such as `status`.

#### Be consistent

Use the same name for the same purpose everywhere. Reuse established coding patterns and conventions. Consistency reduces the reader's cognitive work.

#### Make code obvious

Code is obvious when a reader's first guess about its behaviour is correct. Choose precise names and follow established patterns. Use whitespace to expose structure, and comment only where the code cannot explain itself.

#### Write comments first

Write interface comments before implementation. A method that needs a long descriptive comment has a complex interface and should be redesigned. Comments should preserve information that code cannot represent.

### Reviewing Existing Code

Scan for these red flags in the listed order.

#### Shallow modules

Look for interfaces as complex as their implementations, many trivial methods, or classes with little functionality.

#### Information leakage

Find design decisions repeated across modules. A change to one detail should not require coordinated edits across several classes.

#### Temporal decomposition

Check for code organized around operation order instead of information hiding, such as separate read and write classes for one format.

#### Pass-through methods

Flag methods that only call another method with the same signature, especially when delegation accounts for half or more of a class's methods.

#### Overexposure

A common operation should not force callers to understand rare features. Default information that callers should not have to provide.

#### Conjoined methods

Flag a method when understanding it requires reading another method's implementation.

#### Repetition

Find non-trivial code patterns duplicated in several places.

#### Vague or hard-to-pick names

Flag names broad enough to describe many entities. Difficulty finding a precise name often means the entity has too many responsibilities.

#### Comment problems

Find comments that restate the code or expose implementation details in interface documentation. Long, complicated descriptions may reveal a poor abstraction.

#### Special-general mixture

Keep specialized use-case code out of a general-purpose mechanism.

#### Nonobvious code

Flag behaviour that a quick reading cannot reveal, including surprising side effects.

#### Too many exceptions

Look for exceptions the caller cannot handle and error paths longer than the normal path. Redefine operations when doing so can eliminate error conditions.

For the full checklist, read `references/red-flags.md`.

## References

`references/principles.md` covers all 15 design principles. It includes examples and techniques, along with the reasoning behind each principle. Read it when applying a specific principle or when deeper context is needed.

`references/red-flags.md` organizes every red flag by category. Read it during code review to check systematically for design problems.

# Software Design Review: Desktop App and Sidecar

Scope: `desktop/src/**` (25 non-test TypeScript modules, 3,167 non-test lines) and `sidecar/src/**` (5 modules, 2,584 lines).
Lens: "A Philosophy of Software Design" red-flag checklist.
Method: full read of every prioritised file, plus targeted reads of `backend/src/yinshi/api/auth_routes.py`, `backend/src/yinshi/services/desktop_auth.py`, and the pi SDK `BashOperations` contract.
No files were modified.

## Size and test-coverage baseline

| Module | Lines | Test file | Note |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `sidecar/src/sidecar.js` | 2,021 | none (5 indirect tests in `sidecar/tests/`) | 1 class, 32 methods, 13 responsibilities |
| `desktop/src/main.ts` | 713 | none | 1 function of 342 lines (`configureApplication`) |
| `desktop/src/hostedApiGateway.ts` | 392 | yes | 180-line hand-written route table |
| `desktop/src/hostedAuth.ts` | 365 | yes | |
| `sidecar/src/git_auth.js` | 505 | yes | contains a hand-written shell tokenizer |
| `desktop/src/credentialStore.ts` | 262 | yes | |
| `desktop/src/secureJsonStore.ts` | 170 | none | covered only through `credentialStore.test.ts` |

Untested desktop sources: `main.ts` (713), `secureJsonStore.ts` (170), `signInRenderer.ts` (62), `desktopApi.ts` (51), `preload.ts` (30). The two largest untested files are also the two with the most responsibilities. That correlation is not an accident: both are hard to test because they mix policy with process and window handles.

---

## Part 1: `desktop/src/main.ts` - orchestrator or dumping ground

Verdict: it is a dumping ground with an orchestrator hidden inside it. `DesktopAppController` (`desktop/src/appController.ts:36-149`) is the real orchestrator, and it is clean. `main.ts` is what remains after that extraction stopped halfway.

### Finding D1: main.ts holds eleven distinct responsibilities (severity: high)

Enumerated with line ranges:

1. **Shell environment curation** - `main.ts:67-83`. Chooses which environment variables the child processes inherit, and supplies the fallback `PATH`.
2. **Profile directory naming and creation** - `main.ts:85-105`. Owns the SHA-256 profile identifier and the five-directory layout.
3. **Development executable discovery** - `main.ts:107-128`. Searches `PATH` for `node` and `git`.
4. **Development launch configuration** - `main.ts:130-163`. A second, parallel implementation of `runtimeLaunchConfig.ts`.
5. **Git executable resolution** - `main.ts:165-171`.
6. **Sign-in asset path and shell policy construction** - `main.ts:173-186`.
7. **Window security event wiring** - `main.ts:188-208`.
8. **Window creation and lifetime** - `main.ts:210-235`, plus `main.ts:665-680`.
9. **IPC sender authorisation policy** - `main.ts:237-264`. Decides which page may call which channel.
10. **Dependency composition and the whole sign-in flow** - `main.ts:266-403`, including a 36-line inline sign-in orchestration with its own stage tracking at `main.ts:310-345`.
11. **Eight IPC handlers, one of which is a 104-line business flow** - `main.ts:405-605`. The local-repository import handler at `main.ts:502-605` performs directory selection, clone, a dirty-repository confirmation dialog, a second clone attempt, an HTTP registration call to the local helper, response schema validation, and compensating deletion.
12. **Process startup and update policy** - `main.ts:609-654`, including an update-ready dialog.
13. **Application lifecycle events** - `main.ts:655-713`.

`configureApplication` alone spans `main.ts:266-607`, which is 342 lines in one function. It is not a composition root: composition roots do not contain retry-and-rollback logic (`main.ts:466-481`) or user-facing dialog copy (`main.ts:548-560`).

Concrete restructuring, ordered by payoff:

- `profileLayout.ts`: move `profileDirectoryPath` and `ensureProfileDirectories` (`main.ts:85-105`) next to the layout knowledge in `runtimeLaunchConfig.ts:104-160`. Export one function `profileLayout(userDataPath, userId)` returning the typed directory record used by both. This removes the duplication described in D10.
- `repositoryImportFlow.ts`: move `main.ts:502-605` behind one function `importLocalRepository(deps): Promise<LocalRepositoryImportResult>`, where `deps` supplies `chooseDirectory`, `confirmDirtyImport`, `registerRepository`, and `gitCommand`. The flow then becomes testable without Electron.
- `ipcRouter.ts`: move `requestFromAllowedPage` (`main.ts:237-264`) and all eight `ipcMain.handle` registrations behind `registerDesktopIpc(handlers, policy)`. Each handler currently repeats the same four-line guard plus a `try/catch` rewrap, roughly 30 duplicated lines.
- `signInFlow.ts`: move `main.ts:310-345` into one function that owns the listener lifetime and the stage log.
- `launchConfig` mode parameter: fold `developmentLaunchConfig` (`main.ts:130-163`) into `buildRuntimeLaunchConfig` as `mode: "packaged" | "development"` (see D9).

Target: `main.ts` under 150 lines, containing app-event wiring and one call to a composition function.

---

## Part 2: The session, auth, and lease concept sprawl

This is the most consequential question in the review, so the answer is given in full.

### The six modules and what each actually owns

| Module | Real responsibility | Depth |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `accountLease.ts` (159) | Ed25519 lease token verification and signing-key pinning. Pure, no I/O. | Deep. Good module. |
| `credentialStore.ts` (262) | Multi-profile vault: which profiles exist, which is active, persistence. | Deep. Good module. |
| `secureJsonStore.ts` (170) | Encrypted atomic file with permission checks. | Deep. Good module. |
| `hostedAuth.ts` (365) | The hosted sign-in protocol: PKCE start, browser handoff, token-response parsing. | Deep, but see below. |
| `accountSession.ts` (125) | One function, `resumeDesktopAccount`: refresh the stored profile or fall back to the offline lease. | Shallow-medium. |
| `hostedAccessSession.ts` (99) | In-memory cache of the current access token plus refresh de-duplication. | Shallow. |

### Finding D2: `accountSession` and `hostedAccessSession` are one concept split by operation order (severity: high)

This is textbook temporal decomposition. `accountSession.resumeDesktopAccount` is "what happens at startup and at token expiry". `HostedAccessSession` is "what happens between those moments". Neither owns the account. Both manipulate the same three facts: the active profile, the current access token, and the token expiry.

The split is visible in the wiring. `main.ts:285-292` constructs `HostedAccessSession` with a `resume` callback that calls `resumeDesktopAccount`. `main.ts:301-309` constructs a second, near-identical closure that calls `resumeDesktopAccount` again and then pushes the result into `HostedAccessSession` with `setAccount`. The same operation is expressed twice, in two directions, in the same 25-line region.

The consequence is not only readability. It is a correctness hazard:

- `HostedAccessSession.getAccessToken` (`hostedAccessSession.ts:57-84`) de-duplicates concurrent refreshes with `#refresh` and guards against stale writes with `#epoch`.
- `DesktopAppController.switchProfile` (`appController.ts:110-121`) calls `resumeAccount`, which reaches `resumeDesktopAccount` directly through `main.ts:301-309`, bypassing `#refresh` entirely.
- `resumeDesktopAccount` POSTs the stored refresh token to `auth/desktop/refresh` (`accountSession.ts:88-99`).
- The backend rotates that token and records the old hash in `desktop_used_refresh_tokens` (`backend/src/yinshi/services/desktop_auth.py:270-276`). If a previously rotated token reappears, the backend revokes the whole device (`backend/src/yinshi/services/desktop_auth.py:244-255`).

So two concurrent refreshes with the same stored token do not merely waste a request. The second one is treated as token replay and the device is revoked, which forces a full re-sign-in. The window is reachable: a renderer-initiated `hostedRequest` refresh (`main.ts:295-298`) can overlap with a `switchProfile` IPC call (`main.ts:450-481`) while the application page is live.

Recommended restructuring. Collapse the two modules into one owner and keep the pure parts separate:

```ts
// desktopAccount.ts  (replaces accountSession.ts + hostedAccessSession.ts)
export class DesktopAccount {
  constructor(options: {
    apiBaseUrl: string;
    fetch: FetchAdapter;
    credentialStore: DesktopCredentialStore;
    now?: () => number;
  });

  get profile(): DesktopCredentialProfile | undefined;   // current identity
  resume(): Promise<DesktopAccountState>;                 // startup and profile switch
  accessToken(): Promise<string>;                         // hosted API calls
  adopt(session: HostedDesktopSession): void;             // after interactive sign-in
  clear(): Promise<void>;                                 // sign-out
}
```

All four public operations share one internal serialiser, so every path that spends the stored refresh token is queued behind the same promise. `verifyAccountLease` stays in `accountLease.ts`. `startHostedSignIn` and `readHostedDesktopTokenResponse` stay in `hostedAuth.ts`. The offline-lease fallback (`accountSession.ts:50-70`, `accountSession.ts:100-106`) becomes a private method of `DesktopAccount`, which is where it belongs, because "am I allowed to run offline" is an account question, not a transport question.

Net effect: two modules and two closures in `main.ts` become one module and one field. The refresh-replay hazard is defined out of existence rather than defended against.

`RuntimeSecretStore` (`runtimeSecrets.ts:48-89`) has nothing to do with the user account. It generates and persists three local encryption keys for the Python helper. It shares only the `SecureJsonStore` mechanism. The name places it in the same mental bucket as `credentialStore` and `accountSession`, which is misleading. ## Part 3: Supervisor duplication

### Finding D5: `sidecarSupervisor.ts` and `helperSupervisor.ts` duplicate the process-lifecycle pattern (severity: medium)

Duplicated logic, with citations:

| Concern | Sidecar | Helper |
| --- | --- | --- |
| "is the child alive" | `sidecarSupervisor.ts:73`, `196-198` | `helperSupervisor.ts:24-26`, `124-126` |
| wait-for-exit with timeout | `sidecarSupervisor.ts:71-86` | `helperSupervisor.ts:28-42` |
| SIGTERM, wait, SIGKILL, wait, throw | `sidecarSupervisor.ts:88-100` | `helperSupervisor.ts:44-59` |
| spawn, then readiness, then kill on failure | `sidecarSupervisor.ts:154-186` | `helperSupervisor.ts:99-121` |
| memoised `stop()` | `sidecarSupervisor.ts:189-203` | `helperSupervisor.ts:127-131` |

That is roughly 60 lines of parallel logic. The two copies have already drifted in three ways:

1. Ordering. `helperSupervisor.ts:48-49` registers the exit listener before sending SIGTERM. `sidecarSupervisor.ts:95-96` sends SIGTERM first. Both are currently correct because `waitForExit` re-checks `exitCode`, but a reader must verify that twice.
2. Option shape. `SidecarOptions.args` is `readonly string[]` (`sidecarSupervisor.ts:9`) while `StartManagedHelperOptions.arguments` is `string[]` (`helperSupervisor.ts:17`). Same concept, two names, two mutabilities. `localRuntime.ts:44-52` pays for the mismatch by copying the arrays.
3. Error vocabulary. "sidecar process did not exit after SIGKILL" (`sidecarSupervisor.ts:99`) against "helper did not stop after SIGKILL" (`helperSupervisor.ts:57`).

Recommended restructuring. Extract `childProcessLifecycle.ts` exporting:

```ts
export interface ChildLifecycleOptions {
  readonly command: string;
  readonly args: readonly string[];
  readonly environment: Readonly<Record<string, string>>;
  readonly workingDirectory?: string;
  readonly stdio: StdioOptions;
  readonly startupTimeoutMs: number;
  readonly shutdownTimeoutMs: number;
  readonly awaitReadiness: (child: ChildProcess, signal: AbortSignal) => Promise<Ready>;
  readonly onStarted?: () => Promise<void>;   // sidecar socket permission check
  readonly onStopped?: () => Promise<void>;   // sidecar socket removal
}
export function startSupervisedChild<Ready>(o: ChildLifecycleOptions): Promise<Supervised<Ready>>;
```

`sidecarSupervisor.ts` then keeps only what is genuinely sidecar-specific: stale socket removal (`sidecarSupervisor.ts:43-58`), socket permission assertion (`sidecarSupervisor.ts:60-70`), and the `SOCKET_PATH=` readiness line reader (`sidecarSupervisor.ts:102-152`). `helperSupervisor.ts` keeps only the file-descriptor-3 line reader (`helperSupervisor.ts:61-88`). Estimated reduction: 343 lines becomes about 230, with one copy of the kill sequence.

A worthwhile alternative worth weighing: the two readiness mechanisms are themselves an inconsistency. The sidecar signals readiness by printing `SOCKET_PATH=...` on stdout, the helper by writing JSON on file descriptor 3. Standardising on the descriptor-3 JSON message (`helperProtocol.ts:11-48`) for both children would let one supervisor serve both with no strategy parameter. That is a cross-process protocol change, so it belongs in a separate change from the extraction.

## Part 4: The IPC surface

### Finding D7: the bridge is thin and acceptable, but one channel carries all the weight (severity: low for the bridge, high for the channel)

`preload.ts:9-27` exposes eight methods, each a one-line `ipcRenderer.invoke`. Judged as a set, this is not a wide shallow bridge in the harmful sense. Seven of the eight are genuinely distinct user intents (sign in, sign out, import repository, list profiles, switch profile, remove profile, FileVault status). None of them is an accessor that leaks internal state, and each hides a substantial main-process operation. `desktopApi.ts` correctly holds the shared channel names and payload types, so preload and main cannot drift.

Two real defects in this area:

1. `DesktopProfileSummary` is declared twice, at `credentialStore.ts:22-26` and `desktopApi.ts:29-33`, with identical fields and no structural link. `main.ts:444-449` returns the first through a channel typed with the second. Fix: `desktopApi.ts` should import the type, or `credentialStore.ts` should import it. One line, removes a silent drift path.
2. `fileVaultStatus` (`desktopApi.ts:41`) is the one channel that is a pure accessor for a rarely used display value. It could be folded into an existing "environment status" payload if more such values appear. Not urgent at one instance.

### Finding D8: `hostedApiGateway.routeAllowed` mirrors the backend router by hand (severity: high)

`hostedApiGateway.ts:12-192` is a 180-line route table with 22 inline regular expressions. It restates, in the desktop main process, the URL structure of a backend that lives in `backend/src/yinshi/api/` and currently declares 81 routes. Every backend route addition or rename requires a coordinated edit here, and a mistake fails closed at runtime with the opaque message "Hosted API route is not allowed" (`hostedApiGateway.ts:238`).

This is information leakage in the strict sense: one design decision, the hosted URL space, has two homes in two languages.

The table is not gratuitous. It is a defence-in-depth control that limits what a compromised renderer can reach. So the fix is not deletion. Options, with tradeoffs:

- **Generate the table at build time** from the backend route metadata, for example from the FastAPI OpenAPI document, into `hostedRoutes.generated.ts`. Preserves the control, removes the hand-mirroring, and makes divergence a build failure rather than a runtime rejection. This is the recommended option.
- **Reduce to a coarse policy**: allow `/api/**` and `/auth/providers/**` with method and identifier-shape rules, and rely on the backend for authorisation. Removes about 150 lines but weakens the boundary. Only acceptable if a decision is made that the renderer is trusted.

Whichever is chosen, the query-string rules currently duplicated at `hostedApiGateway.ts:44-66` and again at `hostedApiGateway.ts:180-191` for the provider callback should be stated once.

### Finding D9: development and packaged launch configuration are two implementations of one decision (severity: medium)

`main.ts:130-163` rebuilds the helper and sidecar launch records for development, restating knowledge that `runtimeLaunchConfig.ts` owns: the `--ready-fd 3 --asset-dir` argument shape (`main.ts:143-149` against `runtimeLaunchConfig.ts:165-169`) and the sidecar entry point `sidecar/src/index.js` (`main.ts:154` against `runtimeLaunchConfig.ts:176`). A change to the helper argument list must be made in both places, and only the packaged one is tested (`runtimeLaunchConfig.test.ts`).

Fix: add `mode: "packaged" | "development"` and `projectRoot?: string` to `RuntimeLaunchConfigOptions`, and resolve `command`, `workingDirectory`, and the asset directory inside `buildRuntimeLaunchConfig`. `main.ts` then supplies paths, not structure. Removes 34 lines from `main.ts` and brings the development path under test.

### Finding D10: the profile directory layout is stated in three places (severity: medium)

The five profile subdirectories are created in `main.ts:93-105` (`backups`, `data`, `repositories`, `run`), consumed as environment variables in `runtimeLaunchConfig.ts:104-152`, and re-derived for the import flow in `main.ts:524-527`. Adding a directory means editing two files and hoping the third agrees. Fix as described in D1: one `profileLayout` function returning a typed record, consumed by all three call sites.

### Finding D11: `waitForCallback` declares a parameter that no implementation uses (severity: low)

`hostedAuth.ts:37` declares `waitForCallback: (expectedState: string) => Promise<URL>`. The listener implements `waitForCallback(): Promise<URL>` (`authCallbackListener.ts:11`), and the adapter at `main.ts:331` drops the argument. The state check happens later, inside `validateCallback` (`hostedAuth.ts:150-155`). ### Finding D12: errors are flattened to fixed strings at every boundary (severity: medium)

`main.ts` contains 32 throw sites, and most are of the form `catch { throw new Error("Desktop sign-in failed") }` (`main.ts:322`, `343`, `412`, `421`, `435`, `470`, `477`, `480`, `565`, `587`, `603`). The original error is discarded, and the stage variable is only written to the console (`main.ts:342`). The renderer therefore cannot distinguish "no network" from "credential rejected" from "helper failed to start", and neither can a support log.

The desktop-wide total is 187 throw sites across 3,167 non-test lines, roughly one per 17 lines. Many are internal argument checks on functions whose only callers are inside the same package, for example `appController.ts:19-33`, `hostedAccessSession.ts:19-22`, and `hostedApiGateway.ts:277-284`. In a TypeScript codebase with no external callers, these are duplicated cost without a matching benefit, and they lengthen the error path beyond the normal path.

Recommendation: keep runtime validation at the two true trust boundaries, which are IPC input (`main.ts:405-605`) and anything parsed from disk or network (`credentialStore.ts`, `hostedAuth.ts`, `helperProtocol.ts`). Replace internal `assertDependencies`-style checks with types. Introduce one `DesktopError` carrying a stable `code` so the renderer can branch, and log the cause once at the boundary.

### Finding S2: `processQuery` is 289 lines with a five-flag finalisation state machine (severity: high)

`sidecar.js:1675-1963`. Internal structure:

- 1676-1683: option defaulting.
- 1689-1701: change detection to decide whether to rebuild the pi session.
- 1702-1740: teardown and rebuild.
- 1750-1790: the finalisation machine, using five mutable flags: `agentEndEmitted`, `resultSent`, `pendingResult`, `compactionActive`, `finalizeTimer`.
- 1791-1929: a 139-line event-translation switch over ten pi event types.
- 1930-1942: prompt execution plus the synthetic-result workaround.
- 1943-1962: error handling that must distinguish user cancellation from failure by reading `entry.cancelRequested`, a field written by a different method (`sidecar.js:1970`).

The last point is a conjoined-methods flag: `processQuery`'s catch block cannot be understood without reading `cancelSession`, and `cancelSession` cannot be understood without knowing that `processQuery` clears the flag in two places (`sidecar.js:1932`, `1954`).

The finalisation machine is also the least obvious code in either codebase. `schedulePendingResult` (`sidecar.js:1778-1789`) defers the result by a zero-millisecond timer so that a `compaction_start` arriving in the same turn can cancel it. The reason is real, and the comment at `sidecar.js:1751-1756` explains one half of it, but nothing explains the zero-delay timer, which is the surprising part.

Recommended restructuring. Two extractions, both pure and both directly testable:

```js
// pi/eventTranslator.js  - pure: pi event in, wire messages out
export function translatePiEvent(event, context) { return [ /* messages */ ]; }

// pi/runFinalizer.js  - owns agentEndEmitted, resultSent, pendingResult,
//                       compactionActive, and the deferral timer
export function createRunFinalizer({ emit, buildResult }) {
  return { onEvent(event), onPromptResolved(), onPromptRejected(error) };
}
```

`processQuery` then reduces to roughly 60 lines: resolve the session, subscribe the translator, run the prompt, and report the outcome. The synthetic-result workaround (`sidecar.js:1936-1942`) moves into `onPromptResolved`, where it belongs, and can be tested without a live model.

### Finding S3: `activeSessions` has no removal path (severity: high)

`this.activeSessions` is written at `sidecar.js:1655` and `sidecar.js:1739`, read at `1624`, `1683`, `1966`, and cleared only in `cleanup()` at process exit (`sidecar.js:2005`). There is no `delete`, no time-to-live, and no size cap. Socket close only detaches terminals (`sidecar.js:1129-1132`). The protocol has no session-dispose message: the backend client at `backend/src/yinshi/services/sidecar.py` never sends one.

Each retained entry holds a live pi session with its model context, its settings manager, and an open session file handle from `SessionManager.open` (`sidecar.js:205-235`). In a long-running desktop process, every workspace session ever opened stays resident until quit.

The inconsistency is instructive: the sibling registries do have policies. OAuth flows have a 30-minute time-to-live and a cap of 8 (`sidecar.js:34-35`, `1359-1378`). Terminals are removed on process exit (`sidecar.js:1017-1020`). Only pi sessions have neither.

Recommended fix: give `activeSessions` the same treatment inside a dedicated `pi/sessionRegistry.js`: a maximum entry count, an idle time-to-live, and disposal on eviction that calls `unsubscribe()` and `piSession.dispose()`. Add a `session_release` message to the protocol so the backend can release deterministically.

### Finding S4: the wire field `id` carries four different meanings (severity: medium)

In `handleRequest` (`sidecar.js:1147-1215`), `id` is:

- a pi session identifier for `query`, `warmup`, and `cancel` (`sidecar.js:1201`, `1211`, `1153`);
- a terminal identifier for `terminal_input`, `terminal_resize`, and `terminal_kill` (`sidecar.js:1227`, `1236`, `1245`);
- a workspace identifier fallback for `terminal_attach`, where `options.workspaceId || id` (`sidecar.js:1218`) means the same field may hold either;
- a request correlation identifier for `catalog`, `version`, `list_resources`, `resolve`, and the OAuth messages, where it is routinely replaced by a literal default such as `"catalog"` or `"oauth-start"` (`sidecar.js:1257`, `1385`).

This is a vague name that forced eleven defaulting expressions of the form `id || "something"`. Fix in the protocol module: name the fields `sessionId`, `terminalId`, and `requestId`, and require `requestId` on every request so no handler needs a fallback literal.

### Finding S5: the terminal path is four shallow layers deep (severity: medium)

`handleTerminalAttach` (`sidecar.js:1217-1224`) normalises and calls `attachTerminal` (`1035-1045`), which calls `terminalEntry` (`1024-1033`), which calls `createTerminalEntry` (`976-1022`). ### Finding S6: session reuse is decided by `JSON.stringify` comparison (severity: medium)

`sidecar.js:1689-1694` compares `providerAuth`, `providerConfig`, `gitAuth`, and `settings` by stringifying both sides. ### Finding S7: the same twelve-line error wrapper appears eleven times (severity: medium)

`sidecar.js:1221`, `1230`, `1239`, `1249`, `1262`, `1278`, `1295`, `1321`, `1350`, `1468`, `1527`. Every handler ends with `catch (err) { sendToSocket(socket, { id: id || "...", type: "error", error: err instanceof Error ? err.message : "..." }) }`. That is roughly 90 lines of identical shape.

### Finding S8: `git_auth.js` reimplements shell semantics to make a security decision (severity: medium-high)

`tokenizeShellCommand` (`git_auth.js:65-146`) is a hand-written shell tokenizer, and `parseGitCommandForRuntimeAuth` (`git_auth.js:169-208`) uses it to decide whether a command is a remote git operation that deserves a credential broker. If the parse fails or does not match, the command is handed to pi's real shell instead (`git_auth.js:487`, `492`).

So one string is interpreted by two different parsers with different grammars. The tokenizer is written conservatively, rejecting `$`, `;`, `|`, `>`, `<`, and backticks (`git_auth.js:130-136`), which is the right instinct. The design concern is durability: any future relaxation of that grammar changes which commands receive a one-time GitHub token, and the two interpreters can only be kept in agreement by hand.

The credential handling itself is well designed and should be preserved: a per-command capability on an unlinked file descriptor (`git_auth.js:246-256`), constant-time capability comparison (`git_auth.js:258-271`), single-use credential release (`git_auth.js:311-317`), and a `0600` socket in a `0700` temporary directory (`git_auth.js:210-222`, `330`).

Options:

- **Keep the tokenizer, isolate and document it.** Move it to `shellCommandGrammar.js` with an explicit statement that it is an allow-list recogniser and not a shell, and add table-driven tests for the reject cases. Lowest risk, recommended now.
- **Use the pi SDK `spawnHook`.** `BashToolOptions.spawnHook` (`@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent` `bash.d.ts:47-56`) can rewrite the environment for every command, which would remove the need to recognise git at all. The obstacle is real: the capability is deliberately passed on file descriptor 3, not in the environment, and `spawnHook` only adjusts command, working directory, and environment. Adopting it would require moving the capability into the environment, which makes it readable by every descendant process. Not recommended without a separate threat assessment.

Smaller item: `execOptions` is treated as optional at `git_auth.js:408`, `426`, `441`, `453`, `465` but as required at `git_auth.js:438-439`. The SDK contract makes `options` required, so the optional-chaining is the incorrect half. Pick one and remove the ambiguity.

## Part 6: What is already good

These are worth stating so that a refactor does not damage them.

- `secureJsonStore.ts:100-170` is a genuinely deep module. Atomic temporary-file write, `fsync` on both file and directory, permission assertion before and after, and `O_NOFOLLOW` on read. Its interface is three methods.

Scope: `desktop/src/**` (25 non-test TypeScript modules, 3,167 non-test lines) and `sidecar/src/**` (5 modules, 2,584 lines).

## Size and test-coverage baseline

| Module | Lines | Test file | Note |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `sidecar/src/sidecar.js` | 2,021 | none (5 indirect tests in `sidecar/tests/`) | 1 class, 32 methods, 13 responsibilities |
| `desktop/src/main.ts` | 713 | none | 1 function of 342 lines (`configureApplication`) |
| `desktop/src/hostedApiGateway.ts` | 392 | yes | 180-line hand-written route table |
| `desktop/src/hostedAuth.ts` | 365 | yes | |
| `sidecar/src/git_auth.js` | 505 | yes | contains a hand-written shell tokenizer |
| `desktop/src/credentialStore.ts` | 262 | yes | |
| `desktop/src/secureJsonStore.ts` | 170 | none | covered only through `credentialStore.test.ts` |

Untested desktop sources: `main.ts` (713), `secureJsonStore.ts` (170), `signInRenderer.ts` (62), `desktopApi.ts` (51), `preload.ts` (30). The two largest untested files are also the two with the most responsibilities. That correlation is not an accident: both are hard to test because they mix policy with process and window handles.

---

## Part 1: `desktop/src/main.ts` - orchestrator or dumping ground

Verdict: it is a dumping ground with an orchestrator hidden inside it. `DesktopAppController` (`desktop/src/appController.ts:36-149`) is the real orchestrator, and it is clean. `main.ts` is what remains after that extraction stopped halfway.

### Finding D1: main.ts holds thirteen distinct responsibilities (severity: high)

Enumerated with line ranges:

1. **Shell environment curation** - `main.ts:67-83`. Chooses which environment variables the child processes inherit, and supplies the fallback `PATH`.
2. **Profile directory naming and creation** - `main.ts:85-105`. Owns the SHA-256 profile identifier and the five-directory layout.
3. **Development executable discovery** - `main.ts:107-128`. Searches `PATH` for `node` and `git`.
4. **Development launch configuration** - `main.ts:130-163`. A second, parallel implementation of `runtimeLaunchConfig.ts`.
5. **Git executable resolution** - `main.ts:165-171`.
6. **Sign-in asset path and shell policy construction** - `main.ts:173-186`.
7. **Window security event wiring** - `main.ts:188-208`.
8. **Window creation and lifetime** - `main.ts:210-235`, plus `main.ts:665-680`.
9. **IPC sender authorisation policy** - `main.ts:237-264`. Decides which page may call which channel.
10. **Dependency composition and the whole sign-in flow** - `main.ts:266-403`, including a 36-line inline sign-in orchestration with its own stage tracking at `main.ts:310-345`.
11. **Eight IPC handlers, one of which is a 104-line business flow** - `main.ts:405-605`. The local-repository import handler at `main.ts:502-605` performs directory selection, clone, a dirty-repository confirmation dialog, a second clone attempt, an HTTP registration call to the local helper, response schema validation, and compensating deletion.
12. **Process startup and update policy** - `main.ts:609-654`, including an update-ready dialog.
13. **Application lifecycle events** - `main.ts:655-713`.

`configureApplication` alone spans `main.ts:266-607`, which is 342 lines in one function. It is not a composition root: composition roots do not contain retry-and-rollback logic (`main.ts:466-481`) or user-facing dialog copy (`main.ts:548-560`).

Concrete restructuring, ordered by payoff:

- `profileLayout.ts`: move `profileDirectoryPath` and `ensureProfileDirectories` (`main.ts:85-105`) next to the layout knowledge in `runtimeLaunchConfig.ts:104-160`. Export one function `profileLayout(userDataPath, userId)` returning the typed directory record used by both. This removes the duplication described in D10.
- `repositoryImportFlow.ts`: move `main.ts:502-605` behind one function `importLocalRepository(deps): Promise<LocalRepositoryImportResult>`, where `deps` supplies `chooseDirectory`, `confirmDirtyImport`, `registerRepository`, and `gitCommand`. The flow then becomes testable without Electron.
- `ipcRouter.ts`: move `requestFromAllowedPage` (`main.ts:237-264`) and all eight `ipcMain.handle` registrations behind `registerDesktopIpc(handlers, policy)`. Each handler currently repeats the same four-line guard plus a try-catch rewrap, roughly 30 duplicated lines.
- `signInFlow.ts`: move `main.ts:310-345` into one function that owns the listener lifetime and the stage log.
- `launchConfig` mode parameter: fold `developmentLaunchConfig` (`main.ts:130-163`) into `buildRuntimeLaunchConfig` as `mode: "packaged" | "development"` (see D9).

Target: `main.ts` under 150 lines, containing app-event wiring and one call to a composition function.

### Finding D2: accountSession and hostedAccessSession are one concept split by operation order (severity: high)

This is textbook temporal decomposition.
`resumeDesktopAccount` covers startup and token expiry.
`HostedAccessSession` covers the time between those moments.
Neither module owns the account.
Both manipulate the same three facts: the active profile, the access token, and the expiry.

The split shows up in the wiring.
`main.ts:285-292` builds `HostedAccessSession` with a `resume` callback into `resumeDesktopAccount`.
`main.ts:301-309` builds a second closure that calls `resumeDesktopAccount` and then pushes the result back in.

The cost is not only readability.
It is a correctness hazard:

- `HostedAccessSession.getAccessToken` (`hostedAccessSession.ts:57-84`) de-duplicates refreshes through `#refresh`. It also guards stale writes through `#epoch`.
- `DesktopAppController.switchProfile` (`appController.ts:110-121`) calls `resumeAccount`. That path reaches `resumeDesktopAccount` through `main.ts:301-309` and skips `#refresh`.
- `resumeDesktopAccount` posts the stored refresh token to `auth/desktop/refresh` at `accountSession.ts:88-99`.
- The backend rotates that token and records the old hash at `backend/src/yinshi/services/desktop_auth.py:270-276`.
- A replayed token revokes the whole device at `backend/src/yinshi/services/desktop_auth.py:244-255`.

Two concurrent refreshes therefore do more than waste a request.
The second refresh looks like token replay.
The backend revokes the device, and the user must sign in again.
The window is reachable.
A renderer `hostedRequest` refresh (`main.ts:295-298`) can overlap a `switchProfile` IPC call (`main.ts:450-481`).

```ts
// desktopAccount.ts  (replaces accountSession.ts and hostedAccessSession.ts)
export class DesktopAccount {
  constructor(options: {
    apiBaseUrl: string;
    fetch: FetchAdapter;
    credentialStore: DesktopCredentialStore;
    now?: () => number;
  });

  get profile(): DesktopCredentialProfile | undefined;
  resume(): Promise<DesktopAccountState>;        // startup and profile switch
  accessToken(): Promise<string>;                // hosted API calls
  adopt(session: HostedDesktopSession): void;    // after interactive sign-in
  clear(): Promise<void>;                        // sign-out
}
```

All four operations share one internal queue.
Every path that spends the stored refresh token then waits on the same promise.
`verifyAccountLease` stays in `accountLease.ts`.
`startHostedSignIn` and `readHostedDesktopTokenResponse` stay in `hostedAuth.ts`.
The offline-lease fallback (`accountSession.ts:50-70` and `accountSession.ts:100-106`) becomes private state of `DesktopAccount`.
Offline eligibility is an account question, not a transport question.

Net effect: two modules and two closures become one module and one field.
The replay hazard is defined out of existence instead of defended against.

This is the key question, so the answer is given in full.

### What each module actually owns

| Module | Real responsibility | Depth |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `accountLease.ts` (159) | Ed25519 lease verification and signing-key pinning. No I/O. | Deep. Good module. |
| `credentialStore.ts` (262) | Multi-profile vault, active selection, persistence. | Deep. Good module. |
| `secureJsonStore.ts` (170) | Encrypted atomic file with permission checks. | Deep. Good module. |
| `hostedAuth.ts` (365) | Hosted sign-in protocol and token-response parsing. | Deep. |
| `accountSession.ts` (125) | One function that refreshes, or falls back to the offline lease. | Shallow to medium. |
| `hostedAccessSession.ts` (99) | In-memory access-token cache with refresh de-duplication. | Shallow. |

### Finding D2: accountSession and hostedAccessSession are one concept split by operation order (severity: high)

This is textbook temporal decomposition.
`resumeDesktopAccount` covers startup and token expiry.
`HostedAccessSession` covers the time between those moments.
Neither module owns the account.
Both manipulate the same three facts: the active profile, the access token, and the expiry.

The split shows up in the wiring.
`main.ts:285-292` builds `HostedAccessSession` with a `resume` callback into `resumeDesktopAccount`.
`main.ts:301-309` builds a second closure that calls `resumeDesktopAccount` and then pushes the result back in.
The same operation appears twice, in two directions, inside 25 lines.

The cost is not only readability.
It is a correctness hazard:

- `HostedAccessSession.getAccessToken` (`hostedAccessSession.ts:57-84`) de-duplicates refreshes through `#refresh`. It also guards stale writes through `#epoch`.
- `DesktopAppController.switchProfile` (`appController.ts:110-121`) calls `resumeAccount`. That path reaches `resumeDesktopAccount` through `main.ts:301-309` and skips `#refresh`.
- `resumeDesktopAccount` posts the stored refresh token to `auth/desktop/refresh` at `accountSession.ts:88-99`.
- The backend rotates that token and records the old hash at `backend/src/yinshi/services/desktop_auth.py:270-276`.
- A replayed token revokes the whole device at `backend/src/yinshi/services/desktop_auth.py:244-255`.

Two concurrent refreshes therefore do more than waste a request.
The second refresh looks like token replay.
The backend revokes the device, and the user must sign in again.
The window is reachable.
A renderer `hostedRequest` refresh (`main.ts:295-298`) can overlap a `switchProfile` IPC call (`main.ts:450-481`).

Restructuring: collapse the two modules into one owner.
Keep the pure parts separate.

```ts
// desktopAccount.ts  (replaces accountSession.ts and hostedAccessSession.ts)
export class DesktopAccount {
  constructor(options: {
    apiBaseUrl: string;
    fetch: FetchAdapter;
    credentialStore: DesktopCredentialStore;
    now?: () => number;
  });

  get profile(): DesktopCredentialProfile | undefined;
  resume(): Promise<DesktopAccountState>;        // startup and profile switch
  accessToken(): Promise<string>;                // hosted API calls
  adopt(session: HostedDesktopSession): void;    // after interactive sign-in
  clear(): Promise<void>;                        // sign-out
}
```

All four operations share one internal queue.
Every path that spends the stored refresh token then waits on the same promise.
`verifyAccountLease` stays in `accountLease.ts`.
`startHostedSignIn` and `readHostedDesktopTokenResponse` stay in `hostedAuth.ts`.
The offline-lease fallback (`accountSession.ts:50-70` and `accountSession.ts:100-106`) becomes private state of `DesktopAccount`.
Offline eligibility is an account question, not a transport question.

Net effect: two modules and two closures become one module and one field.
The replay hazard is defined out of existence instead of defended against.

## Part 3: supervisor duplication

### Finding D5: the two supervisors duplicate the process-lifecycle pattern (severity: medium)

| Concern | Sidecar | Helper |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Liveness check | `sidecarSupervisor.ts:73`, `196-198` | `helperSupervisor.ts:24-26`, `124-126` |
| Wait for exit with timeout | `sidecarSupervisor.ts:71-86` | `helperSupervisor.ts:28-42` |
| SIGTERM, wait, SIGKILL, wait, throw | `sidecarSupervisor.ts:88-100` | `helperSupervisor.ts:44-59` |
| Spawn, await readiness, kill on failure | `sidecarSupervisor.ts:154-186` | `helperSupervisor.ts:99-121` |
| Memoised `stop()` | `sidecarSupervisor.ts:189-203` | `helperSupervisor.ts:127-131` |

That is about 60 lines of parallel logic.
The copies have already drifted in three ways:

1. Ordering. `helperSupervisor.ts:48-49` registers the exit listener before SIGTERM. `sidecarSupervisor.ts:95-96` sends SIGTERM first. Both are correct today because `waitForExit` re-checks `exitCode`. A reader must verify that twice.
2. Option shape. `SidecarOptions.args` is `readonly string[]` at `sidecarSupervisor.ts:9`. `StartManagedHelperOptions.arguments` is `string[]` at `helperSupervisor.ts:17`. One concept, two names, two mutabilities. `localRuntime.ts:44-52` pays for that by copying arrays.
3. Error vocabulary. Compare `sidecarSupervisor.ts:99` with `helperSupervisor.ts:57`.

Restructuring: extract `childProcessLifecycle.ts`.

```ts
export interface ChildLifecycleOptions<Ready> {
  readonly command: string;
  readonly args: readonly string[];
  readonly environment: Readonly<Record<string, string>>;
  readonly workingDirectory?: string;
  readonly stdio: StdioOptions;
  readonly startupTimeoutMs: number;
  readonly shutdownTimeoutMs: number;
  readonly awaitReadiness: (child: ChildProcess, signal: AbortSignal) => Promise<Ready>;
  readonly onStarted?: () => Promise<void>;   // sidecar socket permission check
  readonly onStopped?: () => Promise<void>;   // sidecar socket removal
}
export function startSupervisedChild<Ready>(o: ChildLifecycleOptions<Ready>): Promise<Supervised<Ready>>;
```

`sidecarSupervisor.ts` then keeps only sidecar-specific parts.
Those are stale socket removal (`sidecarSupervisor.ts:43-58`), the permission assertion (`sidecarSupervisor.ts:60-70`), and the readiness line reader (`sidecarSupervisor.ts:102-152`).
`helperSupervisor.ts` keeps only the descriptor-3 line reader at `helperSupervisor.ts:61-88`.
Estimated size change: 343 lines become about 230.

A second option deserves weighing.
The two readiness mechanisms are themselves inconsistent.
The sidecar prints `SOCKET_PATH=...` on stdout.
The helper writes JSON on file descriptor 3.
One shared descriptor-3 message (`helperProtocol.ts:11-48`) would remove the strategy parameter.
That is a cross-process protocol change, so it belongs in a separate change.

## Part 4: the IPC surface

### Finding D7: the bridge is thin, but one channel carries the weight (severity: low for the bridge, high for the channel)

`preload.ts:9-27` exposes eight methods.
Each is a one-line `ipcRenderer.invoke`.
As a set this is not a harmful wide bridge.
Seven of the eight are distinct user intents.
None is an accessor that leaks internal state.
Each hides a substantial main-process operation.
`desktopApi.ts` holds shared channel names and payload types, so preload and main cannot drift.

Two real defects here:

1. `DesktopProfileSummary` is declared twice. See `credentialStore.ts:22-26` and `desktopApi.ts:29-33`. The fields are identical and the two types have no structural link. `main.ts:444-449` returns the first through a channel typed with the second. Fix by importing one from the other.
2. `fileVaultStatus` at `desktopApi.ts:41` is a pure accessor for a rare display value. Fold it into a wider status payload if more such values appear. It is not urgent at one instance.

### Finding D8: hostedApiGateway mirrors the backend router by hand (severity: high)

`hostedApiGateway.ts:12-192` is a 180-line route table with 22 inline regular expressions.
It restates the hosted URL space inside the desktop main process.
The backend declares 81 routes under `backend/src/yinshi/api/`.
Every backend route change needs a matching edit here.
A miss fails closed at runtime with the message "Hosted API route is not allowed" at `hostedApiGateway.ts:238`.

This is information leakage in the strict sense.
One decision, the hosted URL space, has two homes in two languages.

The table is not gratuitous.
It limits what a compromised renderer can reach.
So deletion is the wrong fix.
Options and tradeoffs:

- Generate the table at build time from the backend OpenAPI document into `hostedRoutes.generated.ts`. This keeps the control and removes hand-mirroring. Divergence becomes a build failure instead of a runtime rejection. This is the recommended option.
- Reduce to a coarse policy over `/api/**` and `/auth/providers/**` with method and identifier rules. This removes about 150 lines but weakens the boundary. Choose it only after deciding that the renderer is trusted.

Either way, state the query rules once.
They are currently duplicated at `hostedApiGateway.ts:44-66` and `hostedApiGateway.ts:180-191`.

### Finding D9: development and packaged launch configuration are duplicated (severity: medium)

`main.ts:130-163` rebuilds the helper and sidecar launch records for development.
It restates knowledge owned by `runtimeLaunchConfig.ts`.
Compare the argument shape at `main.ts:143-149` with `runtimeLaunchConfig.ts:165-169`.
Compare the sidecar entry point at `main.ts:154` with `runtimeLaunchConfig.ts:176`.
A helper argument change needs edits in both places.
Only the packaged path has tests, in `runtimeLaunchConfig.test.ts`.

Fix: add `mode: "packaged" | "development"` and `projectRoot?: string` to `RuntimeLaunchConfigOptions`.
Resolve `command`, `workingDirectory`, and the asset directory inside `buildRuntimeLaunchConfig`.
`main.ts` then supplies paths, not structure.
This removes 34 lines from `main.ts` and brings the development path under test.

### Finding D10: the profile layout is stated in three places (severity: medium)

The five subdirectories are created at `main.ts:93-105`.
They are consumed as environment variables at `runtimeLaunchConfig.ts:104-152`.
They are re-derived for the import flow at `main.ts:524-527`.
Adding a directory means editing two files and trusting the third.

### Finding D11: waitForCallback declares an unused parameter (severity: low)

`hostedAuth.ts:37` declares `waitForCallback: (expectedState: string) => Promise<URL>`.
The listener implements `waitForCallback(): Promise<URL>` at `authCallbackListener.ts:11`.
The adapter at `main.ts:331` drops the argument.
State validation happens later, inside `validateCallback` at `hostedAuth.ts:150-155`.
The interface implies a contract that no implementation honours.

### Finding D12: errors are flattened to fixed strings at every boundary (severity: medium)

`main.ts` has 32 throw sites.
Most take the form `catch { throw new Error("Desktop sign-in failed") }`.
See `main.ts:322`, `343`, `412`, `421`, `435`, `470`, `477`, `480`, `565`, `587`, and `603`.
The original error is discarded.
The stage value is written only to the console at `main.ts:342`.
The renderer cannot separate a network failure from a rejected credential or a failed helper start.
Support logs cannot either.

The desktop total is 187 throw sites across 3,167 non-test lines.
That is about one per 17 lines.
Many are internal argument checks with only in-package callers.
See `appController.ts:19-33`, `hostedAccessSession.ts:19-22`, and `hostedApiGateway.ts:277-284`.
In typed code with no external callers these add cost without matching benefit.
They also make the error path longer than the normal path.

Recommendation: keep runtime validation at the two true trust boundaries.
Those are IPC input (`main.ts:405-605`) and anything parsed from disk or network.
Replace internal dependency assertions with types.
Add one `DesktopError` carrying a stable `code` so the renderer can branch.
Log the cause once, at the boundary.

### Finding S2: processQuery is 289 lines with a five-flag finalisation machine (severity: high)

`processQuery` spans `sidecar.js:1675-1963`.
Internal structure:

- `1676-1683`: option defaulting.
- `1689-1701`: change detection that decides whether to rebuild the pi session.
- `1702-1740`: teardown and rebuild.
- `1750-1790`: the finalisation machine with five mutable flags. Those are `agentEndEmitted`, `resultSent`, `pendingResult`, `compactionActive`, and `finalizeTimer`.
- `1791-1929`: a 139-line translation switch over ten pi event types.
- `1930-1942`: prompt execution and the synthetic-result workaround.
- `1943-1962`: error handling that separates cancellation from failure.

The last part is a conjoined-methods flag.
The catch block reads `entry.cancelRequested`, which `cancelSession` writes at `sidecar.js:1970`.
`cancelSession` in turn depends on `processQuery` clearing the flag at `sidecar.js:1932` and `sidecar.js:1954`.
Neither method can be understood alone.

The finalisation machine is the least obvious code in either codebase.
`schedulePendingResult` at `sidecar.js:1778-1789` defers the result with a zero-millisecond timer.
That lets a `compaction_start` in the same turn cancel the pending result.
The comment at `sidecar.js:1751-1756` explains the inline-command half.
Nothing explains the zero-delay timer, which is the surprising part.

Restructuring: two extractions, both pure and both testable.

```js
// pi/eventTranslator.js - pure. pi event in, wire messages out.
export function translatePiEvent(event, context) { return [ /* messages */ ]; }

// pi/runFinalizer.js - owns the five flags and the deferral timer.
export function createRunFinalizer({ emit, buildResult }) {
  return { onEvent(event), onPromptResolved(), onPromptRejected(error) };
}
```

`processQuery` then drops to about 60 lines.
It resolves the session, subscribes the translator, runs the prompt, and reports the outcome.
The synthetic-result workaround at `sidecar.js:1936-1942` moves into `onPromptResolved`.
It can then be tested without a live model.

### Finding S3: activeSessions has no removal path (severity: high)

`activeSessions` is written at `sidecar.js:1655` and `sidecar.js:1739`.
It is read at `sidecar.js:1624`, `1683`, and `1966`.
It is cleared only in `cleanup()` at `sidecar.js:2005`, which runs at process exit.
There is no delete, no time-to-live, and no size cap.
Socket close only detaches terminals at `sidecar.js:1129-1132`.
The protocol has no dispose message, and `backend/src/yinshi/services/sidecar.py` never sends one.

Each retained entry holds a live pi session.
That includes model context, a settings manager, and a session file handle from `SessionManager.open` at `sidecar.js:205-235`.
In a long-running desktop process, every session opened stays resident until quit.

The inconsistency is instructive.
OAuth flows have a 30-minute time-to-live and a cap of 8. See `sidecar.js:34-35` and `sidecar.js:1359-1378`.
Terminals are removed on exit at `sidecar.js:1017-1020`.
Only pi sessions have neither policy.

Fix: move the map into `pi/sessionRegistry.js`.
Add a maximum entry count and an idle time-to-live.
On eviction, call `unsubscribe()` and `piSession.dispose()`.
Add a `session_release` message so the backend can release deterministically.

### Finding S4: the wire field `id` carries four meanings (severity: medium)

Inside `handleRequest` at `sidecar.js:1147-1215`, `id` is:

- a pi session identifier for `query`, `warmup`, and `cancel`. See `sidecar.js:1201`, `1211`, and `1153`.
- a terminal identifier for `terminal_input`, `terminal_resize`, and `terminal_kill`. See `sidecar.js:1227`, `1236`, and `1245`.
- a workspace identifier fallback for `terminal_attach` at `sidecar.js:1218`, where `options.workspaceId || id` allows either.
- a request correlation identifier for `catalog`, `version`, `list_resources`, `resolve`, and the OAuth messages.

The correlation case is routinely replaced by a literal default.
See `sidecar.js:1257` and `sidecar.js:1385`.
The vague name forced eleven `id || "something"` expressions.
Fix in the protocol module.
Name the fields `sessionId`, `terminalId`, and `requestId`.
Require `requestId` on every request so no handler needs a fallback literal.

### Finding S5: the terminal path is four shallow layers deep (severity: medium)

`handleTerminalAttach` (`sidecar.js:1217-1224`) calls `attachTerminal` (`1035-1045`).
That calls `terminalEntry` (`1024-1033`), which calls `createTerminalEntry` (`976-1022`).
The middle two layers add three lines each.
`handleTerminalInput` (`1226-1233`), `handleTerminalResize` (`1235-1242`), and `handleTerminalKill` (`1244-1252`) are normalise-and-delegate wrappers.
Six of 32 methods have that shape.

Fix: move the registry into `terminals/terminalRegistry.js`.

The dispatch table then calls the registry directly, and one layer disappears.

### Finding S6: session reuse is decided by JSON.stringify comparison (severity: medium)

`sidecar.js:1689-1694` compares `providerAuth`, `providerConfig`, `gitAuth`, and `settings` by stringifying both sides.
The comparison is key-order sensitive.
A different key order from the backend tears down the pi session and rebuilds it.
The warm context is then lost for no reason.
The code is also non-obvious, because nothing states that the check is structural.

Fix: compute one `sessionFingerprint(options)` inside the session registry.
Derive it from an explicit ordered list of rebuild-forcing fields.

### Finding S7: the same error wrapper appears eleven times (severity: medium)

See `sidecar.js:1221`, `1230`, `1239`, `1249`, `1262`, `1278`, `1295`, `1321`, `1350`, `1468`, and `1527`.

### Finding S8: git_auth reimplements shell semantics for a security decision (severity: medium-high)

`tokenizeShellCommand` at `git_auth.js:65-146` is a hand-written shell tokenizer.
`parseGitCommandForRuntimeAuth` at `git_auth.js:169-208` uses it.
It decides whether a command is a remote git operation that deserves a credential broker.
On a parse failure or a non-match, the command goes to the real shell.
See `git_auth.js:487` and `git_auth.js:492`.

So one string is interpreted by two parsers with different grammars.
The tokenizer is conservative and rejects `$`, `;`, `|`, `>`, `<`, and backticks at `git_auth.js:130-136`.
That instinct is right.
The design concern is durability.
Any future relaxation changes which commands receive a one-time GitHub token.
The two interpreters can only be kept in agreement by hand.

The credential handling itself is well designed and should be preserved.
It uses a per-command capability on an unlinked descriptor at `git_auth.js:246-256`.
It compares capabilities in constant time at `git_auth.js:258-271`.
It releases the credential once at `git_auth.js:311-317`.
It uses a `0600` socket inside a `0700` temporary directory. See `git_auth.js:210-222` and `git_auth.js:330`.

Options:

- Keep the tokenizer and isolate it. Move it to `shellCommandGrammar.js`. State that it is an allow-list recogniser, not a shell. Add table-driven reject tests. This is the lowest-risk option and is recommended now.
- Use the pi SDK `spawnHook` from `BashToolOptions`. It rewrites the environment for every command and would remove the need to recognise git. The obstacle is real. The capability is deliberately passed on descriptor 3, not in the environment. `spawnHook` adjusts only command, working directory, and environment. Moving the capability into the environment exposes it to every descendant process. Do not adopt this without a separate threat assessment.

Smaller item: `execOptions` is optional at `git_auth.js:408`, `426`, `441`, `453`, and `465`.
It is required at `git_auth.js:438-439`.
The SDK contract makes `options` required, so the optional chaining is the wrong half.
Pick one and remove the ambiguity.

### Finding S9: the connection read buffer is unbounded (severity: medium)

`sidecar.js:1116-1120` appends chunks with no length ceiling.

The socket is `0600` and same-user at `sidecar.js:1089`, so the impact is a local defect, not an attack.

# Software Design Review: Desktop App and Sidecar

Scope: `desktop/src/**` and `sidecar/src/**`.
Desktop has 25 non-test modules and 3,167 non-test lines.
Sidecar has 5 modules and 2,584 lines.
Lens: the red-flag checklist from "A Philosophy of Software Design".
Method: full read of every prioritised file.
Cross-checks: `backend/src/yinshi/api/auth_routes.py`, `backend/src/yinshi/services/desktop_auth.py`, and the pi SDK `BashOperations` contract.
No files were modified.

## Size and test baseline

| Module | Lines | Test file | Note |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `sidecar/src/sidecar.js` | 2,021 | none direct | 1 class, 32 methods, 13 responsibilities |
| `desktop/src/main.ts` | 713 | none | one 342-line function |
| `desktop/src/hostedApiGateway.ts` | 392 | yes | 180-line hand-written route table |
| `desktop/src/hostedAuth.ts` | 365 | yes | |
| `sidecar/src/git_auth.js` | 505 | yes | hand-written shell tokenizer |
| `desktop/src/credentialStore.ts` | 262 | yes | |
| `desktop/src/secureJsonStore.ts` | 170 | none | covered only through `credentialStore.test.ts` |

Desktop sources with no test file: `main.ts` (713), `secureJsonStore.ts` (170), `signInRenderer.ts` (62), `desktopApi.ts` (51), `preload.ts` (30).

The two largest untested files also hold the most responsibilities.
That correlation is not an accident.
Both mix policy with process handles and window handles, so both resist testing.

---

## Part 1: main.ts responsibilities

Verdict: `main.ts` is a dumping ground with an orchestrator hidden inside it.
`DesktopAppController` at `desktop/src/appController.ts:36-149` is the real orchestrator.
That module is clean.
`main.ts` is the residue left after the extraction stopped halfway.

### Finding D1: main.ts holds thirteen responsibilities (severity: high)

1. Shell environment curation at `main.ts:67-83`. It picks inherited variables and the fallback `PATH`.
2. Profile directory naming and creation at `main.ts:85-105`. It owns the SHA-256 profile identifier and the five-directory layout.
3. Development executable discovery at `main.ts:107-128`. It searches `PATH` for `node` and `git`.
4. Development launch configuration at `main.ts:130-163`. This is a second implementation of `runtimeLaunchConfig.ts`.
5. Git executable resolution at `main.ts:165-171`.
6. Sign-in asset path and shell policy construction at `main.ts:173-186`.
7. Window security event wiring at `main.ts:188-208`.
8. Window creation and lifetime at `main.ts:210-235` and `main.ts:665-680`.
9. IPC sender authorisation policy at `main.ts:237-264`. It decides which page may call which channel.
10. Dependency composition at `main.ts:266-403`. This includes a 36-line inline sign-in flow at `main.ts:310-345`.
11. Eight IPC handlers at `main.ts:405-605`.
12. Process startup and update policy at `main.ts:609-654`. This includes update-ready dialog copy.
13. Application lifecycle events at `main.ts:655-713`.

Item 11 hides a full business flow.
The local repository import handler at `main.ts:502-605` is 104 lines.
It performs directory selection, clone, dirty-repository confirmation, and a second clone attempt.
It then calls the local helper over HTTP.
It validates the response shape and deletes the clone on failure.

`configureApplication` spans `main.ts:266-607`, which is 342 lines in one function.
This is not a composition root.
Composition roots do not hold rollback logic (`main.ts:466-481`) or dialog copy (`main.ts:548-560`).

Restructuring, ordered by payoff:

- Add `profileLayout.ts`. Move `profileDirectoryPath` and `ensureProfileDirectories` from `main.ts:85-105`. Place them beside the layout knowledge in `runtimeLaunchConfig.ts:104-160`. Export one function `profileLayout(userDataPath, userId)`. This also fixes D10.
- Add `repositoryImportFlow.ts`. Move `main.ts:502-605` behind one function. Inject `chooseDirectory`, `confirmDirtyImport`, `registerRepository`, and `gitCommand`. The flow then becomes testable without Electron.
- Add `ipcRouter.ts`. Move `requestFromAllowedPage` (`main.ts:237-264`) and the eight registrations. Each handler repeats a four-line guard and a rewrap. That is about 30 duplicated lines.
- Add `signInFlow.ts`. Move `main.ts:310-345` into one function. It owns the listener lifetime and the stage log.
- Fold `developmentLaunchConfig` (`main.ts:130-163`) into `buildRuntimeLaunchConfig`. Add a `mode` parameter. See D9.

Target size for `main.ts`: under 150 lines.
It should hold app-event wiring and one composition call.

---

## Part 2: session, auth, and lease concept sprawl

This is the key question, so the answer is given in full.

### What each module actually owns

| Module | Real responsibility | Depth |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `accountLease.ts` (159) | Ed25519 lease verification and signing-key pinning. No I/O. | Deep. Good module. |
| `credentialStore.ts` (262) | Multi-profile vault, active selection, persistence. | Deep. Good module. |
| `secureJsonStore.ts` (170) | Encrypted atomic file with permission checks. | Deep. Good module. |
| `hostedAuth.ts` (365) | Hosted sign-in protocol and token-response parsing. | Deep. |
| `accountSession.ts` (125) | One function. It refreshes, or falls back to the offline lease. | Shallow to medium. |
| `hostedAccessSession.ts` (99) | In-memory access-token cache with refresh de-duplication. | Shallow. |

### Finding D2: accountSession and hostedAccessSession are one concept split by operation order (severity: high)

This is textbook temporal decomposition.
`resumeDesktopAccount` covers startup and token expiry.
`HostedAccessSession` covers the time between those moments.
Neither module owns the account.
Both manipulate the same three facts.
Those are the active profile, the access token, and the expiry.

The split shows up in the wiring.
`main.ts:285-292` builds `HostedAccessSession` with a `resume` callback into `resumeDesktopAccount`.
`main.ts:301-309` builds a second closure.
That closure calls `resumeDesktopAccount` and pushes the result back in.
The same operation appears twice, in two directions, inside 25 lines.

The cost is not only readability.
It is a correctness hazard:

- `HostedAccessSession.getAccessToken` (`hostedAccessSession.ts:57-84`) de-duplicates refreshes through `#refresh`. It guards stale writes through `#epoch`.
- `DesktopAppController.switchProfile` (`appController.ts:110-121`) calls `resumeAccount`. That path reaches `resumeDesktopAccount` through `main.ts:301-309`. It skips `#refresh`.
- `resumeDesktopAccount` posts the stored refresh token at `accountSession.ts:88-99`.
- The backend rotates that token and records the old hash at `backend/src/yinshi/services/desktop_auth.py:270-276`.
- A replayed token revokes the whole device at `backend/src/yinshi/services/desktop_auth.py:244-255`.

Two concurrent refreshes therefore do more than waste a request.
The second refresh looks like token replay.
The backend revokes the device, and the user must sign in again.
The window is reachable.
A renderer `hostedRequest` refresh (`main.ts:295-298`) can overlap a `switchProfile` call (`main.ts:450-481`).

Restructuring: collapse the two modules into one owner.
Keep the pure parts separate.

```ts
// desktopAccount.ts replaces accountSession.ts and hostedAccessSession.ts
export class DesktopAccount {
constructor(options: { apiBaseUrl: string; fetch: FetchAdapter; credentialStore: DesktopCredentialStore; now?: () => number });
get profile(): DesktopCredentialProfile | undefined;
resume(): Promise<DesktopAccountState>;
accessToken(): Promise<string>;
adopt(session: HostedDesktopSession): void;
clear(): Promise<void>;
}
```

All four operations share one internal queue.
Every path that spends the stored refresh token then waits on the same promise.
`verifyAccountLease` stays in `accountLease.ts`.
`startHostedSignIn` and `readHostedDesktopTokenResponse` stay in `hostedAuth.ts`.
The offline-lease fallback becomes private state of `DesktopAccount`.
See `accountSession.ts:50-70` and `accountSession.ts:100-106`.
Offline eligibility is an account question, not a transport question.

Net effect: two modules and two closures become one module and one field.
The replay hazard is defined out of existence instead of defended against.

### Finding D3: runtimeSecrets is named as if it joined the auth cluster (severity: low)

`RuntimeSecretStore` at `runtimeSecrets.ts:48-89` has no link to the user account.
It generates three local encryption keys for the Python helper.
It shares only the `SecureJsonStore` mechanism.
The name places it beside `credentialStore` and `accountSession` in the reader's mind.
Suggested rename: `helperKeyStore.ts` with `HelperKeyStore`.
The values are consumed only as helper environment variables at `runtimeLaunchConfig.ts:140-151`.

### Finding D4: runtime-secret validation has two homes (severity: medium)

`validateRuntimeSecrets` exists twice with identical regular expressions.
See `runtimeSecrets.ts:20-46` and `runtimeLaunchConfig.ts:72-82`.
The second copy exists because `buildRuntimeLaunchConfig` does not trust its caller.
Export the validator once and import it.
A branded `RuntimeSecrets` type produced only by the store also works.

---

## Part 3: supervisor duplication

### Finding D5: the two supervisors duplicate the process-lifecycle pattern (severity: medium)

| Concern | Sidecar | Helper |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Liveness check | `sidecarSupervisor.ts:73`, `196-198` | `helperSupervisor.ts:24-26`, `124-126` |
| Wait for exit with timeout | `sidecarSupervisor.ts:71-86` | `helperSupervisor.ts:28-42` |
| SIGTERM, wait, SIGKILL, wait, throw | `sidecarSupervisor.ts:88-100` | `helperSupervisor.ts:44-59` |
| Spawn, await readiness, kill on failure | `sidecarSupervisor.ts:154-186` | `helperSupervisor.ts:99-121` |
| Memoised `stop()` | `sidecarSupervisor.ts:189-203` | `helperSupervisor.ts:127-131` |

That is about 60 lines of parallel logic.
The copies have already drifted in three ways:

1. Ordering. `helperSupervisor.ts:48-49` registers the exit listener before SIGTERM. `sidecarSupervisor.ts:95-96` sends SIGTERM first. Both are correct today, because `waitForExit` re-checks `exitCode`. A reader must verify that twice.
2. Option shape. `SidecarOptions.args` is `readonly string[]` at `sidecarSupervisor.ts:9`. `StartManagedHelperOptions.arguments` is `string[]` at `helperSupervisor.ts:17`. One concept, two names, two mutabilities. `localRuntime.ts:44-52` pays for that by copying arrays.
3. Error vocabulary. Compare `sidecarSupervisor.ts:99` with `helperSupervisor.ts:57`.

Restructuring: extract `childProcessLifecycle.ts`.

```ts
export interface ChildLifecycleOptions<Ready> {
readonly command: string;
readonly args: readonly string[];
readonly environment: Readonly<Record<string, string>>;
readonly workingDirectory?: string;
readonly stdio: StdioOptions;
readonly startupTimeoutMs: number;
readonly shutdownTimeoutMs: number;
readonly awaitReadiness: (child: ChildProcess, signal: AbortSignal) => Promise<Ready>;
readonly onStarted?: () => Promise<void>;
readonly onStopped?: () => Promise<void>;
}
export function startSupervisedChild<Ready>(o: ChildLifecycleOptions<Ready>): Promise<Supervised<Ready>>;
```

`onStarted` carries the sidecar socket permission check.
`onStopped` carries the sidecar socket removal.
`sidecarSupervisor.ts` then keeps only sidecar-specific parts.
Those are stale socket removal (`sidecarSupervisor.ts:43-58`), the permission assertion (`sidecarSupervisor.ts:60-70`), and the readiness reader (`sidecarSupervisor.ts:102-152`).
`helperSupervisor.ts` keeps only the descriptor-3 reader at `helperSupervisor.ts:61-88`.
Estimated size change: 343 lines become about 230.

A second option deserves weighing.
The two readiness mechanisms are themselves inconsistent.
The sidecar prints `SOCKET_PATH=...` on stdout.
The helper writes JSON on file descriptor 3.
One shared descriptor-3 message (`helperProtocol.ts:11-48`) would remove the strategy parameter.
That is a cross-process protocol change, so it belongs in a separate change.

### Finding D6: localRuntime is a thin pass-through with one real idea (severity: low)

`startLocalRuntime` at `localRuntime.ts:19-98` forwards `ready` and `processId` at `localRuntime.ts:66-67`.
Its real value is the combined `running` getter (`localRuntime.ts:68-70`) and the ordered shutdown (`localRuntime.ts:71-96`).
The socket-path cross-check at `localRuntime.ts:22-29` is a symptom.
It re-verifies an invariant that `buildRuntimeLaunchConfig` already guarantees.
The check exists because `main.ts:130-163` can break that invariant.
After D9 lands, the check becomes dead defence.

---

## Part 4: the IPC surface

### Finding D7: the bridge is thin, but one channel carries the weight (severity: low for the bridge, high for the channel)

`preload.ts:9-27` exposes eight methods.
Each is a one-line `ipcRenderer.invoke`.
As a set this is not a harmful wide bridge.
Seven of the eight are distinct user intents.
None is an accessor that leaks internal state.
Each hides a substantial main-process operation.
`desktopApi.ts` holds shared channel names and payload types, so preload and main cannot drift.

Two real defects here:

1. `DesktopProfileSummary` is declared twice. See `credentialStore.ts:22-26` and `desktopApi.ts:29-33`. The fields are identical, and the types have no structural link. `main.ts:444-449` returns the first through a channel typed with the second. Fix by importing one from the other.
2. `fileVaultStatus` at `desktopApi.ts:41` is a pure accessor for a rare display value. Fold it into a wider status payload if more such values appear. It is not urgent at one instance.

### Finding D8: hostedApiGateway mirrors the backend router by hand (severity: high)

`hostedApiGateway.ts:12-192` is a 180-line route table with 22 inline regular expressions.
It restates the hosted URL space inside the desktop main process.
The backend declares 81 routes under `backend/src/yinshi/api/`.
Every backend route change needs a matching edit here.
A miss fails closed at runtime with the message at `hostedApiGateway.ts:238`.

This is information leakage in the strict sense.
One decision, the hosted URL space, has two homes in two languages.

The table is not gratuitous.
It limits what a compromised renderer can reach.
So deletion is the wrong fix.
Options and tradeoffs:

- Generate the table at build time from the backend OpenAPI document into `hostedRoutes.generated.ts`. This keeps the control and removes hand-mirroring. Divergence becomes a build failure, not a runtime rejection. This is the recommended option.
- Reduce to a coarse policy over `/api/**` and `/auth/providers/**`. Use method rules and identifier-shape rules. This removes about 150 lines, but it weakens the boundary. Choose it only after deciding that the renderer is trusted.

Either way, state the query rules once.
They are currently duplicated at `hostedApiGateway.ts:44-66` and `hostedApiGateway.ts:180-191`.

### Finding D9: development and packaged launch configuration are duplicated (severity: medium)

`main.ts:130-163` rebuilds the helper and sidecar launch records for development.
It restates knowledge owned by `runtimeLaunchConfig.ts`.
Compare the argument shape at `main.ts:143-149` with `runtimeLaunchConfig.ts:165-169`.
Compare the sidecar entry point at `main.ts:154` with `runtimeLaunchConfig.ts:176`.
A helper argument change needs edits in both places.
Only the packaged path has tests, in `runtimeLaunchConfig.test.ts`.

Fix: add `mode` and `projectRoot` to `RuntimeLaunchConfigOptions`.
Resolve `command`, `workingDirectory`, and the asset directory inside `buildRuntimeLaunchConfig`.
`main.ts` then supplies paths, not structure.
This removes 34 lines from `main.ts`.
It also brings the development path under test.

### Finding D10: the profile layout is stated in three places (severity: medium)

The five subdirectories are created at `main.ts:93-105`.
They are consumed as environment variables at `runtimeLaunchConfig.ts:104-152`.
They are re-derived for the import flow at `main.ts:524-527`.
Adding a directory means editing two files and trusting the third.
Fix through the `profileLayout` function described in D1.

### Finding D11: waitForCallback declares an unused parameter (severity: low)

`hostedAuth.ts:37` declares `waitForCallback: (expectedState: string) => Promise<URL>`.
The listener implements `waitForCallback(): Promise<URL>` at `authCallbackListener.ts:11`.
The adapter at `main.ts:331` drops the argument.
State validation happens later, inside `validateCallback` at `hostedAuth.ts:150-155`.
The interface implies a contract that no implementation honours.
Fix: drop the parameter from the type.
Central state validation in `hostedAuth.ts` is correct.

### Finding D12: errors are flattened to fixed strings at every boundary (severity: medium)

`main.ts` has 32 throw sites.
Most discard the cause and throw a fixed string.
See `main.ts:322`, `343`, `412`, `421`, `435`, `470`, `477`, `480`, `565`, `587`, and `603`.
The stage value is written only to the console at `main.ts:342`.
The renderer cannot separate a network failure from a rejected credential.
It also cannot separate either one from a failed helper start.
Support logs face the same limit.

The desktop total is 187 throw sites across 3,167 non-test lines.
That is about one per 17 lines.
Many are internal argument checks with only in-package callers.
See `appController.ts:19-33`, `hostedAccessSession.ts:19-22`, and `hostedApiGateway.ts:277-284`.
In typed code with no external callers, these add cost without matching benefit.
They also make the error path longer than the normal path.

Recommendation: keep runtime validation at the two true trust boundaries.
Those are IPC input (`main.ts:405-605`) and anything parsed from disk or network.
Replace internal dependency assertions with types.
Add one `DesktopError` carrying a stable `code` so the renderer can branch.
Log the cause once, at the boundary.

---

## Part 5: sidecar.js responsibilities and decomposition

`YinshiSidecar` at `sidecar.js:932-2021` is one class of 1,090 lines.
It has 32 methods and three independent registries at `sidecar.js:934-936`.
Above it sit 900 lines of module-level helpers.
The class name is the first red flag.
"The sidecar" is a process, not a concept.

### Finding S1: thirteen responsibilities in one file (severity: high)

| # | Responsibility | Lines | Approximate size |

### Finding D7: the bridge is thin, but one channel carries the weight (severity: low for the bridge, high for the channel)

### Finding D8: hostedApiGateway mirrors the backend router by hand (severity: high)

`hostedApiGateway.ts:12-192` is a 180-line route table with 22 inline regular expressions.

The backend declares 81 routes under `backend/src/yinshi/api/`.

A miss fails closed at runtime with the message at `hostedApiGateway.ts:238`.

This is information leakage in the strict sense.
One decision, the hosted URL space, has two homes in two languages.

The table is not gratuitous.
It limits what a compromised renderer can reach.
So deletion is the wrong fix.
Options and tradeoffs:

- Generate the table at build time from the backend OpenAPI document into `hostedRoutes.generated.ts`. This keeps the control and removes hand-mirroring. Divergence becomes a build failure, not a runtime rejection. This is the recommended option.
- Reduce to a coarse policy over `/api/**` and `/auth/providers/**`. Use method rules and identifier-shape rules. This removes about 150 lines, but it weakens the boundary. Choose it only after deciding that the renderer is trusted.

Either way, state the query rules once.
They are currently duplicated at `hostedApiGateway.ts:44-66` and `hostedApiGateway.ts:180-191`.
